$comment: Project-specific guidance for the Kurdish tokenizer paper. Everything here is a recommendation, not an ARO rule, except where 'aro' lists requirement ids. No results are stated or implied: placeholders in examples are written as [X].
summary: A study of tokenization for Kurdish in large language models: BPE and Unigram tokenizers trained across several vocabulary sizes and training-data distributions (including dialect mixes), compared with the tokenizers of existing pretrained models.

sections.name: Title and index terms
sections.purpose: Tell an engineer outside NLP what you compared and on which language.
sections.evidence: None; it must match what the Results show.
content: Name the language (and dialects if central), the algorithms and the setting (LLMs).
Avoid acronyms in the title unless unavoidable.
sections.example: Tokenizing Kurdish for Large Language Models: Byte-Pair Encoding and Unigram across Vocabulary Sizes and Dialect Mixes (16 words; cut one).

sections.name: Abstract
sections.purpose: Let the editor decide in one read whether the paper is worth reviewing.
sections.evidence: Only findings that appear in Results, with the same numbers.
content: Why: tokenizers built for high-resource languages split Kurdish into many pieces, which costs context and compute.
What and how: the grid you trained and the metrics you used.
Findings: your two or three main results, with numbers.
Significance: what a model builder should do differently.
sections.example: Large language models process Kurdish with tokenizers trained mostly on other languages, which [X]. We train byte-pair encoding and Unigram tokenizers at [N] vocabulary sizes on [M] training mixtures of Sorani, Kurmanji and [...], and compare them with the tokenizers of [K] pretrained models using fertility, [...] …

sections.name: Introduction
sections.purpose: Show the gap and state the contribution, with no subheadings.
sections.evidence: Citations to peer-reviewed work on Kurdish NLP, tokenization and multilingual tokenizer fairness.
content: Kurdish: speakers, dialects, scripts (Arabic-based for Sorani, Latin for Kurmanji), and why that complicates tokenization.
Why tokenization matters for LLM cost and quality.
What earlier Kurdish and low-resource tokenizer work did and did not cover.
A short list of contributions, each pointing to a result.
sections.example: Contributions: (1) the first systematic comparison of [...] for Kurdish at vocabulary sizes from [a] to [b]; (2) …

sections.name: Materials and Methods
sections.purpose: Let another team reproduce every number.
sections.evidence: Corpus statistics, cleaning steps, exact training settings, metric definitions.
content: Corpora: sources, licences, sizes before and after deduplication, dialect and script shares.
Normalisation: Unicode form, character unification (e.g. Arabic vs Persian code points), script handling, punctuation.
Tokenizer training: library and version, algorithm settings, character coverage, byte fallback, special tokens, seeds.
Experimental grid: algorithms × vocabulary sizes × data distributions.
Baselines: which pretrained tokenizers and why.
Metrics as numbered equations: fertility, compression, unknown-token or byte-fallback rate, [...].
Held-out evaluation sets per dialect and script.
Compute: hardware and time.
sections.example: Fertility is the mean number of tokens per word: F = T / W   (1), where T is the number of tokens and W the number of whitespace-separated words in the evaluation set.
done: Every corpus has source, licence and size
Every metric is defined as a numbered equation

sections.name: Results and Discussion
sections.purpose: Report what happened, then explain it.
sections.evidence: Tables and figures for every comparison claimed; variance or significance where you claim a difference.
content: Effect of vocabulary size per algorithm.
Effect of data distribution and dialect share.
Comparison with pretrained tokenizers.
Segmentation analysis on examples (morpheme boundaries).
Downstream effect, if you measured it.
Limitations: dialect coverage, corpus domain, metrics that do not capture quality.
sections.example: Titles that state the finding: 'Fig. 3. Fertility falls with vocabulary size for both algorithms, flattening after [X]'.
done: Every claim cites a figure or table
Within the figure cap for your word band

sections.name: Conclusions
sections.purpose: State what a practitioner should take away, and what is next.
content: Main findings in a few sentences.
Practical recommendation (e.g. vocabulary size range).
Future work: downstream training, more dialects, release.

sections.name: Acknowledgment
sections.purpose: Credit funding, compute and data providers; disclose interests.
content: Funding and grants.
Compute provider.
Corpus providers and annotators.
Conflicts of interest, if any.
sections.example: S. A. Author thanks [...] for access to [...].
done: Omitted from the anonymised copy if it identifies you

sections.name: References
content: Harvard author-date, alphabetical.
Peer-reviewed versions of tokenization papers (ACL Anthology).
DOIs or URLs.
Datasets and software cited where the licence asks.

topics.name: Kurdish language characteristics and morphology
topics.note: Agglutinative morphology, clitics and dialect variation shape how subword units should look.

topics.name: Corpus collection, deduplication and normalisation
topics.note: Report sizes before and after; near-duplicate removal changes vocabulary statistics.

topics.name: Dialect and script coverage
topics.note: Sorani (Arabic-based script), Kurmanji (Latin script) and others; report per-dialect evaluation.

topics.name: Tokenization algorithms
topics.note: BPE and Unigram; state the implementation and settings.

topics.name: Vocabulary-size experiments
topics.note: Choose sizes that bracket typical LLM vocabularies; include the largest sizes you trained.

topics.name: Training data distributions
topics.note: Vary dialect shares deliberately; describe each mixture exactly.

topics.name: Baseline tokenizer comparisons
topics.note: Name the pretrained models, their tokenizer versions and how you obtained them.

topics.name: Compression and fertility metrics
topics.note: Define each metric as an equation; use the same evaluation text for all tokenizers.

topics.name: Unknown-token and byte-fallback behaviour
topics.note: Report how often each tokenizer falls back to bytes or unknown tokens per script.

topics.name: Morphological segmentation analysis
topics.note: Qualitative examples plus, if available, agreement with a morpheme-segmented sample.

topics.name: Computational efficiency
topics.note: Training and encoding time with hardware stated, in seconds.

topics.name: Downstream language-model evaluation
topics.note: Optional but strengthens claims about LLM impact; state if out of scope.

topics.name: Statistical analysis and reproducibility
topics.note: Seeds, repeated runs or bootstrap intervals where you claim one setting beats another.

topics.name: Research limitations
topics.note: Corpus domain, dialects not covered, metrics that do not measure quality.

topics.name: Public release of code, models and artifacts
topics.note: Release where corpus licences permit; link it from the paper after acceptance (keep it anonymous during review).

matrix.claim: Tokenizer A segments Kurdish more efficiently than tokenizer B
matrix.evidence: Fertility and compression on the same held-out text, per dialect and script

matrix.claim: A vocabulary size of [X] is a good trade-off
matrix.evidence: Metric curves across all trained sizes, plus model-side cost (embedding size)
matrix.strength: Show the curve flattening, not one point

matrix.claim: Dialect share in training changes performance
matrix.evidence: Per-dialect metrics for each training mixture
matrix.strength: Same evaluation sets for every mixture

matrix.claim: Existing LLM tokenizers handle Kurdish poorly
matrix.evidence: Baseline tokenizers on the same evaluation sets, with versions named

matrix.claim: Segments align better with Kurdish morphology
matrix.evidence: Segmentation examples and, ideally, agreement with a morpheme-annotated sample
matrix.strength: Annotated sample size and annotator agreement

matrix.evidence: A downstream experiment (perplexity per byte, task accuracy) holding everything else fixed
matrix.strength: Without it, describe the claim as a hypothesis

matrix.evidence: Full settings, seeds, corpus sources and code release plan
